How was Trump’s proposed border wall discussed in his 2019 tweets?

Text Analysis Project Showcase · November 3, 2026

Author

Maricia Marquez · POLS 4130 · Fall 2026

Research question

How did Donald Trump discuss the proposed U.S.–Mexico border wall in his 2019 tweets, and how did the sentiment and recurring themes of wall-related tweets compare with his broader Twitter communication?

Data

This project analyzes 4,469 tweets posted by Donald Trump between January 1 and December 31, 2019.

The dataset (trump_tweets_2019.csv) contains one tweet per observation.

Tweets were classified as wall-related if their text contained at least one of the following terms or phrases: “wall,” “barrier,” “fence,” “border security,” “southern border,” “caravan,” or “shutdown.”

  • 237 wall-related tweets (5.3%)
  • 4,232 other tweets (94.7%)

Methods

Sentiment analysis: I used the Bing Liu sentiment dictionary, which assigns positive polarity (+1) and negative polarity (−1) to matched words. I applied a two-word negation rule to account for negators preceding sentiment-bearing words. I calculated sentiment scores across entire tweets and within a four-word target window surrounding references to “wall.”

Topic modeling: I used Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) to identify recurring themes across the 2019 corpus. Tweets were tokenized, converted to lemmas, and stripped of SMART stopwords and selected additional terms. I selected four topics (k = 4) and interpreted them using prominent keywords and representative tweets.

The document-term matrix retained 4,434 tweets. Thirty-five tweets with no retained words were excluded from topic modeling.

Word frequency

The most frequently used terms provide an overview of recurring language in Trump’s 2019 tweets.

The top words for each of the four estimated topics, extracted from the fitted LDA model.

Sentiment findings

Wall-related tweets exhibited more negative dictionary sentiment than other tweets.

Using the negation-adjusted measure, wall-related tweets had an average sentiment score of −0.203, compared with +0.328 for other tweets.

This difference indicates that wall-related tweets contained a more negative balance of sentiment-bearing words. However, dictionary-based sentiment measures word-level polarity, not Trump’s overall position toward the border wall.

Mean negation-adjusted Bing Liu sentiment score per tweet. Negative scores indicate more negative than positive matched words; they do not necessarily indicate opposition to the wall.

Basic sentiment comparison

Mean basic dictionary sentiment scores by tweet category, before applying the negation adjustment.

Sentiment surrounding “wall”

Among wall-related tweets with a target-window match, the average sentiment score was −0.0295 across 81 matches. No other-group tweets had a target-window match.

This score was close to 0, suggesting that negative sentiment across border-related tweets was not necessarily concentrated near explicit references to the word “wall.”

Examining the original tweets

Sentiment example — Tweet 112

“The damage done to our Country from a badly broken Border - Drugs, Crime and so much that is bad - is far greater than a Shutdown…”

Tweet 112 received a net sentiment score of −5 because the dictionary identified five negative words: damage, badly, broken, crime, and bad.

Trump used this negative language to characterize border conditions and argue for addressing the situation.

This illustrates the difference between negative vocabulary and the overall political message of a tweet.

Limitations

Sentiment: Dictionary-based analysis cannot reliably identify sarcasm, complex rhetoric, context, or the target of a statement. Negative language may describe border conditions rather than express opposition to a border-wall policy. Dictionary coverage was limited: 8.17% of words in wall-related tweets and 11.5% of words in other tweets matched the sentiment dictionary. Target-window results were based on 81 matches.

Topics: LDA identifies patterns of word co-occurrence rather than objectively defined subjects. Tweets can address multiple themes, and topic labels require researcher interpretation. Results also depend on preprocessing decisions and the selected number of topics (k = 4). Differences in average topic proportions are descriptive and were not tested for statistical significance.

Topic findings

The LDA model identified four recurring themes:

  1. Foreign Policy & National Interests
  2. Partisan Politics & Elections
  3. Border Security & Economic Promises
  4. Media Criticism & Fake News

Wall-related tweets had a higher average proportion of Topic 3 (Border Security & Economic Promises) than other tweets: 30.1% compared with 24.6%.

The other three topics were less represented in the wall-related group.

Sentiment by topic

Answer to the research question

Trump’s wall-related tweets differed from his broader 2019 communication in both sentiment vocabulary and thematic emphasis. Wall-related tweets had a more negative average dictionary sentiment score, while topic modeling showed a greater emphasis on border security and economic promises.

Together, these findings suggest that Trump’s border-related messaging frequently framed the issue through negative descriptions of border conditions and arguments about security and economic interests.

Sources:

  • Trump, Donald J. (2019). 2019 Twitter corpus. Supplied course dataset, trump_tweets_2019.csv.
  • Bing Liu. Opinion Mining, Sentiment Analysis, and Opinion Spam Detection. Sentiment dictionary supplied as bing_liu_dictionary.csv.
  • Topic modeling and text preprocessing conducted in R using tidytext, textstem, slider, and topicmodels.
